items.prompt: What is the main body of a fungus, the part that does most of its living and feeding?

options.label: The mushroom cap that appears above ground
options.feedback: The cap is only a temporary structure built for reproduction; the fungus spends most of its life as something else entirely.

options.label: A spreading network of thread-like hyphae
options.feedback: This tangled network, called a mycelium, spreads through soil or wood and is what every later mushroom grows out of.

options.label: A single large cell buried in the soil
options.feedback: A fungus is not one large cell; its body is built from many thin threads growing and branching together.

options.label: The spores waiting to be released
options.feedback: Spores are how the fungus spreads to new places, not the feeding, growing body of the organism itself.

items.ok_line: The mushroom is just the visitor; the threads are the resident.
items.ko_title: Not the part you can see
items.ko_line: Most of a fungus is out of sight, spread through the soil or wood around it.
items.exp_title: A web of threads doing the real work
items.exp_text: A fungus spends nearly all of its life as a mass of thin threads called hyphae, which spread through soil, wood, or dead leaves, branching and rebranching until they form a tangled network called a mycelium. Every mushroom that later appears above ground grows out of this hidden network, using it as a base rather than being the organism itself.

items.prompt: How does a fungus manage to feed without a mouth or a stomach?

options.label: It photosynthesizes food using sunlight
options.feedback: A fungus has no chlorophyll and cannot capture light for energy; it must get its food from somewhere else entirely.

options.label: It swallows tiny particles whole through its cell walls
options.feedback: A fungal cell wall does not open to let solid particles through; whatever crosses it has to already be dissolved.

options.label: It filters nutrients out of rainwater
options.feedback: Rainwater carries almost nothing worth filtering; a fungus gets its food from the material it is growing on, not from the water passing over it.

options.label: It releases enzymes onto its food, then absorbs the dissolved result
options.feedback: Breaking the food down outside its own body lets the fungus absorb only the simple molecules small enough to cross back through its hyphal wall.

items.ok_line: It breaks the food down before taking any of it in.
items.ko_line: A fungus has no inside space to digest food in — so where could that step actually happen?
items.exp_text: A fungus pumps digestive enzymes out of its hyphae directly onto whatever it is growing on, and those enzymes break the surrounding material down into simple molecules small enough to pass back through the hyphal wall. Because the breaking-down happens outside the fungus's own body rather than inside it, a fungus can only feed on whatever it is already touching, which is why its threads keep growing outward in search of fresh material.

items.prompt: What is a mushroom, in relation to the fungus that grew it?

options.label: A temporary structure built only to reproduce
options.feedback: It exists purely to lift spore-producing surfaces into the open air, then decays once the spores are released.

options.label: The fungus's main feeding organ
options.feedback: Feeding is handled by the underground network of hyphae, not by the mushroom that appears above the surface.

options.label: A young fungus that has not yet spread underground
options.feedback: The mushroom does not come before the underground network — the network is already established and mature by the time a mushroom appears.

options.label: A separate fungus growing on top of the real one
options.feedback: The mushroom is not a second organism; it is part of the very same fungus that produced it.

items.ok_line: It exists just long enough to send spores out into the world.
items.ko_line: The mushroom is a short-lived structure with one specific purpose, not the fungus's ordinary way of living.
items.exp_title: A structure raised for a single purpose
items.exp_text: When conditions favor releasing spores, a fungus's underground network diverts its resources into building a compact, fast-growing structure that pushes up above the surface — the mushroom — purely to lift its spore-producing surfaces into the open air. Once the spores have been released, that structure has served its purpose and decays, while the underground network that built it carries on growing exactly as it did before.

items.prompt: Why does a mushroom cap have thin gills lining its underside instead of a smooth surface?

options.label: Gills let rainwater drain away from the spores
options.feedback: Gills are not drainage channels; their arrangement has nothing to do with directing water away.

options.label: Gills help the cap stay rigid in wind
options.feedback: The cap's rigidity comes from its overall structure, not from the thin gills, which are far too delicate to be doing that job.

options.label: Gills multiply the surface area available for producing spores
options.feedback: Folding the spore-producing layer into many blades packs far more producing surface into the same small cap.

options.label: Gills store extra food for the mycelium below
options.feedback: Gills are not a storage structure; nothing about their thin, folded shape is suited to holding a food reserve.

items.ok_line: Folding the surface is how it fits so much into so little space.
items.ko_title: Think about surface, not support or drainage
items.ko_line: The gills exist to pack in as much spore-producing surface as possible.
items.exp_title: Folded to fit more spores in less space
items.exp_text: Each thin gill under a mushroom cap is coated in cells that release spores, and by folding this spore-producing layer into many closely spaced blades rather than leaving it flat, a mushroom packs a far larger producing surface into the same small cap. As the spores mature they drop straight down out of the gaps between the gills and drift off on any passing current of air.

items.prompt: How does a mycorrhizal fungus help a tree get water and minerals from soil that the tree's own roots cannot reach?

options.label: It stores rainwater in underground pockets for the tree to draw on later
options.feedback: The fungus is not a storage tank; it delivers what it finds directly, rather than holding a reserve for later use.

options.label: Its thread-like hyphae reach farther into the soil than root hairs can and pass nutrients back to the roots
options.feedback: The fungus's threads extend well beyond the tree's own root hairs and pass back whatever water and minerals they find in exchange for sugar.

options.label: It dissolves the tree's own roots to release trapped nutrients
options.feedback: The fungus does not break down the tree's living roots; the partnership works because both sides stay intact and cooperate.

options.label: It pulls moisture from the air and drips it onto the roots
options.feedback: The fungus is working underground in the soil, not gathering moisture from the air above it.

items.ok_line: Threads finer than roots can go where roots cannot.
items.ko_line: This partnership works because the fungus's threads extend the tree's reach through the soil itself.
items.exp_title: Threads that extend a tree's reach
items.exp_text: A mycorrhizal fungus wraps its hyphae around or inside a tree's finest roots and then sends those same threads spreading much farther through the soil than any root hair could grow, reaching pockets of water and minerals the tree alone would never touch. What the fungus finds out there it passes back to the tree through the connection at the root, and in return the tree supplies the fungus with sugar it has no way to make for itself.

items.prompt: Why doesn't a fungus turn green the way a plant does when it grows in sunlight?

options.label: It has no chlorophyll and gets its food by absorption instead
options.feedback: With no light-capturing pigment in its cells, a fungus feeds by absorbing nutrients rather than making food from sunlight.

options.label: It grows too fast for chlorophyll to build up
options.feedback: Speed of growth has nothing to do with pigment; a slow-growing fungus is just as colorless as a fast-growing one.

options.label: Sunlight destroys chlorophyll in a fungus's cells
options.feedback: There is no chlorophyll present in a fungus's cells to begin with, so there is nothing there for sunlight to destroy.

options.label: Fungi only grow in the dark, away from sunlight
options.feedback: Plenty of fungi grow in full daylight without any trouble; darkness is not a requirement for them.

items.ok_line: A fungus feeds by absorbing, not by catching light.
items.ko_title: It isn't about speed, damage, or darkness
items.ko_line: The real reason is simpler: the fungus was never built to use light for food in the first place.
items.exp_title: A different way of feeding entirely
items.exp_text: Chlorophyll exists in a plant's cells to capture the energy of light and turn it into food, and a fungus never evolved that pigment because it gets its food a completely different way, by absorbing nutrients already broken down from dead or living material around it. With no light-capturing pigment in its cells, a fungus growing in bright sun looks exactly as pale or brown as one growing in total darkness.

items.prompt: How does a puffball mushroom release its cloud of spores into the air?

options.label: It splits open on its own once the spores inside mature
options.feedback: A mature puffball does not simply split open by itself; something has to trigger the release at the right moment.

options.label: Wind alone is strong enough to blow the spores out through its skin
options.feedback: Ordinary wind cannot force spores through the puffball's tough outer skin; something more direct is needed to push them out.

options.label: Animals dig it up and scatter the spores while eating it
options.feedback: Being dug up and eaten is not the usual trigger; a puffball is built to release its spores without needing to be disturbed by an animal at all.

options.label: The impact of a raindrop or a touch squeezes the ball, forcing spores out through a pore
options.feedback: Any sudden pressure on the thin sac forces a puff of spore-laden air out through the single small opening at its top.

items.ok_line: One tap and the cloud goes up.
items.ko_line: The puffball needs a physical push from outside to force the spores out.
items.exp_title: A cloud released by a single tap
items.exp_text: A ripe puffball is a tough, thin-walled sac packed with a fine powder of spores and a single small opening at the top, so any sudden pressure — a falling raindrop, a footstep, an animal brushing past — squeezes the sac and forces a puff of air and spores out through that opening. The lighter the touch and the drier the ball, the farther the resulting cloud of spores can drift once it escapes.

items.prompt: Why do mushrooms often seem to appear overnight after rain, when the fungus that made them was already there?

options.label: Rain washes fungal spores in from somewhere else
options.feedback: The mushrooms are not arriving from elsewhere; they grow directly from the fungus's own network that was already present underground.

options.label: The fungus only starts growing once it rains
options.feedback: The fungus itself was already alive and growing in the soil well before the rain; the rain does not start its growth from scratch.

options.label: Moisture triggers the underground network to build fruiting structures quickly
options.feedback: A good soaking of rain signals a mycelium that has been quietly growing for a long time to suddenly build a mushroom, swelling mostly by filling with water rather than growing new tissue.

options.label: Rain physically pushes the mushrooms up out of the ground
options.feedback: Rain does not mechanically shove anything upward; the mushroom grows up under its own power once it begins forming.

items.ok_line: The network was ready — it was only waiting for the cue.
items.ko_line: The fungus wasn't created by the rain; the rain only told it the moment had come.
items.exp_title: A network waiting for its moment
items.exp_text: The underground mycelium of a fungus can spend a long stretch of time quietly growing through soil or wood with no visible sign above the surface, storing up enough resources to build a mushroom the moment conditions turn favorable. A good soaking of rain is often exactly that signal, and because a mushroom is built mostly of cells rapidly filling with water rather than growing new tissue from scratch, it can swell to full size while the ground around it is still drying out.

items.prompt: How does a single yeast cell reproduce?

options.label: It splits cleanly down the middle into two equal cells
options.feedback: That even splitting in half is how many other single-celled organisms divide, but it is not how a yeast cell makes a new one.

options.label: A small bulge grows on its side and pinches off as a new cell
options.feedback: The bulge enlarges, receives a copy of the nucleus, and pinches off once it has grown enough machinery to survive alone.

options.label: It releases spores that drift away and grow independently
options.feedback: Producing spores is a separate strategy some fungi use, but it is not the everyday way an ordinary yeast cell makes more of itself.

options.label: It fuses with a neighboring cell to form a larger one
options.feedback: Fusing with a neighbor would produce one larger cell, not the growing population that yeast is known for; that is not how it multiplies.

items.ok_line: A small bulge becomes a whole new cell.
items.ko_line: The new cell doesn't form by dividing the original one down the middle.
items.exp_title: A cell that buds off its own copy
items.exp_text: A yeast cell grows a small bulge on its outer surface, and as that bulge enlarges the cell's nucleus divides and one copy moves into it, so the bulge becomes a fully equipped cell in its own right rather than an empty scrap. Once it has grown enough internal machinery to survive alone, the bud pinches off from its parent entirely, leaving behind a small scar on the original cell where the connection used to be.

items.prompt: How does a mold spread across an entire loaf of bread so quickly once it takes hold?

options.label: Its threads keep extending at their tips and branching into new territory
options.feedback: Thousands of growing tips push forward through the bread at once, each releasing enzymes just ahead of itself and absorbing the result.

options.label: It releases a gas that carries spores through the loaf
options.feedback: No gas is doing the carrying; the mold's own threads are what physically extend through the bread.

options.label: The bread's own yeast turns into mold as it goes stale
options.feedback: Mold is a completely different organism from any yeast in the bread; one does not transform into the other.

options.label: It waits until the whole loaf is stale before growing at all
options.feedback: Mold does not wait for staleness; it can begin growing on fresh bread as soon as a spore lands and finds enough moisture.

items.ok_title: Growing at the tip, again and again
items.ok_line: Every branch is another front line pushing outward.
items.ko_title: Not gas, not a transformation, not a wait
items.ko_line: What's spreading through the bread is the mold's own threads, physically extending forward.
items.exp_text: A mold's hyphae grow only at their very tips, but each thread branches again and again as it extends, so what looks like a single colony is really thousands of growing tips all pushing forward through the bread at once. Every one of those tips releases digestive enzymes into the fresh bread just ahead of it and absorbs the result, which is how the mold can spread across a whole loaf while never actually growing anywhere but at its own advancing edges.
